places.name: France
places.note: In France, so much of public life still happens in person: at a café table, in a market line, around a meal that is allowed to take its time. Since 2017, labor law has also recognized a right to disconnect, so work messages are not assumed to follow people home.

cards.title: The apéritif
cards.body: The gastronomic meal of the French, inscribed by UNESCO in 2010, customarily opens with an apéritif — a pause that gathers people before the meal begins.

cards.title: Service Civique
cards.body: Through Service Civique, young people in France can spend six to twelve months on a mission of general interest — in education, the environment, culture, solidarity, and other civic fields.

cards.title: The right to disconnect
cards.body: Since 1 January 2017, French labor law has required companies to address employees’ droit à la déconnexion — the right not to be expected to answer work messages during rest, leave, and family life.

cards.title: Terroir
cards.body: Terroir is more than “soil.” In French it names the living bond between a place — its land, climate, and know-how — and the taste of what is grown or made there.

cards.title: A meal that gathers
cards.body: UNESCO recognized the gastronomic meal of the French not as luxury dining, but as a social ritual for celebrating important moments, meant to draw family and friends closer together.

places.name: Spain
places.note: Spain is too often flattened into sun, spectacle, and a long afternoon sleep. After a meal, sobremesa keeps people at the table just to talk; in the evening, the paseo turns a street into a shared living room.

cards.title: Sobremesa
cards.body: The Real Academia Española defines sobremesa as the time spent at the table after eating. It is not leftover food — it is leftover time, kept for conversation.

cards.title: Erasmus in Spain
cards.body: Spain has consistently been among the top — and often the leading — destinations for Erasmus+ higher-education exchanges, a meeting place for young people from across Europe.

cards.title: The siesta myth
cards.body: Travel posts and stock images still sell a Spain that sleeps through the afternoon. In a 2009 Fundadeps survey of more than 3,000 adults, 58.6% said they never took a siesta, and only 16.2% did so daily.

cards.title: Quedar
cards.body: In everyday Spanish, quedar is how you make a plan to meet someone. It is a small word for a big habit: showing up for one another, in person.

cards.title: Tapeo
cards.body: A tapa is a small portion of food, often shared. Going for tapas — tapeo — is a way of eating in company, moving from plate to plate and conversation to conversation.

places.name: Italy
places.note: Italy is easy to reduce to one plate of pasta and one famous tower, but connection often happens at a walking pace: a passeggiata in the evening, an aperitivo before the meal. Slow Food, which began here, is one way people have pushed back against speed and sameness at the table.

cards.title: Passeggiata
cards.body: A passeggiata is a stroll, often in the evening along a main street or a seafront — a way of taking the air, greeting neighbors, and taking part in the life of a town.

cards.title: Servizio Civile Universale
cards.body: Since a 2017 reform, Italy’s Servizio Civile Universale has invited young people (ages 18–28) into unarmed civic service, on projects for communities, education, and peace.

cards.title: Slow Food
cards.body: Slow Food began in Italy in 1986, after protests against a fast-food restaurant near Rome’s Spanish Steps, and became an international movement in 1989. It argues for food that is “good, clean and fair,” a reply to a system — and, today, to feeds — that push the same flavors everywhere.

cards.title: Convivio
cards.body: In Italian, a convivio is a banquet, a being-together at the table (from the Latin convivium, “to live together”). It names the meal as a place of company, not only of calories.

cards.title: Aperitivo
cards.body: An aperitivo is the drink — and the accompanying bites — that opens the evening. It is less a cocktail hour than a social pause: a way of arriving, together, before the meal.

places.name: India
places.note: In India, a meal can be a thali of many complementary dishes, and a greeting like namaste acknowledges the person in front of you. A vast generation of young people is already changing how the country pays, speaks, and is seen — including through public systems such as UPI.

cards.title: Mysuru Dasara
cards.body: Mysuru Dasara, also called Nada Habba, is Karnataka’s ten-day state festival, ending on Vijayadashami. The royal city fills with processions, music, and light.

cards.title: A vast generation
cards.body: United Nations population estimates show India as home to the world’s largest population of young people (ages 15–24) — a generation already shaping culture, technology, and public life.

cards.title: UPI
cards.body: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), run by NPCI, is India’s instant, interoperable public payments system. It has become everyday infrastructure for households and small merchants. Large digital systems can widen access; they also raise questions about privacy, inclusion, and who is left out if the technology fails.

cards.title: Namaste
cards.body: Namaste is a widely used greeting in India, often made with the palms together, that acknowledges the person in front of you. In a project about listening, it is a useful word to carry: attention is a form of respect.

cards.title: The thali
cards.body: A South Indian thali arrives as a spread of complementary dishes — often on a banana leaf — to be eaten together, with the hand, as a complete meal rather than a single main course.

places.name: Mexico
places.note: Día de Muertos is not Halloween in another language. It is a way families stay in conversation with those they love, building ofrendas of food, flowers, and light. This is a travel postcard, for now.

photos.alt: Pan de muerto, marigold flowers, candles, and food on a Día de Muertos ofrenda
photos.caption_html: Pan de muerto, cempasúchil, candles, and food on a Día de Muertos ofrenda. Photo: Wotancito, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 (cropped and resized).

photos.caption_html: The Baja California Sur coast from the air, on the approach to Los Cabos. Photo: Mirror Project

cards.title: Día de Muertos
cards.body: As practiced especially in Mexico’s Indigenous communities, Día de Muertos commemorates the temporary return of relatives and loved ones each year in late October and early November. UNESCO inscribed the festivity in 2008.

cards.title: Ley Olimpia
cards.body: The campaign known as Ley Olimpia, begun by Olimpia Coral Melo after her intimate images were shared without consent, helped Mexico criminalize digital sexual violence. It is one way young people have pushed for dignity in digital life.

cards.title: Not a costume
cards.body: Feeds and stock imagery often flatten Día de Muertos into a generic Halloween look. The practice UNESCO describes is a family ritual of welcome — food, flowers, candles, and memory — not a costume.

cards.title: Ofrenda
cards.body: An ofrenda is the home or cemetery altar prepared for Día de Muertos: food, flowers, candles, and photographs arranged so the dead can find their way.

cards.title: A table for a visit
cards.body: Families prepare the deceased’s favorite dishes and place them on the ofrenda alongside bread, fruit, and flowers — a table set for a visit, not only a farewell. Pan de muerto is part of that welcome.

places.name: England
places.note: England is more than palaces and pageantry. People connect over a Sunday roast, in a local pub, and in the open-air argument of Speakers’ Corner — a living public culture, not a souvenir myth.

cards.title: Speakers’ Corner
cards.body: At the north-east edge of Hyde Park, Speakers’ Corner continues a long tradition of public debate. The 1872 Parks Regulation Act established the right to meet and speak freely in the park.

cards.title: UK Youth Parliament
cards.body: Young people aged 11 to 18 can be elected as Members of Youth Parliament, who represent their areas and take debates into the House of Commons chamber.
cards.source_label: UK Parliament / House of Commons Library

cards.title: Online Safety Act
cards.body: The Online Safety Act 2023 places duties of care on major online platforms, including additional protections for children — a reminder that technology is not neutral, and that the rules around it can be argued in public.

cards.title: Cheers
cards.body: In everyday British English, “cheers” can mean thank you, goodbye, or a toast — a small word that does a lot of social work.

cards.title: Sunday roast
cards.body: A shared meal of roast meat, potatoes, vegetables, and often Yorkshire pudding — a weekly table that still gathers families and friends, at home or in the local pub.

places.name: Singapore
places.note: Look past the glass and efficiency, and Singapore is also a community dining room. In hawker centres, people from many backgrounds share a table; young people are among those training to keep that culture going.

cards.title: Hawker culture
cards.body: Hawker centres serve as community dining rooms, where people from many backgrounds gather over food. UNESCO inscribed Singapore’s hawker culture in 2020.

cards.title: Incubation stalls
cards.body: Singapore’s Incubation Stall Programme helps aspiring hawkers, including people new to the trade, start a stall at reduced rent — one way a new generation can keep hawker culture going.

cards.title: Smart Nation
cards.body: Singapore’s Smart Nation programme uses digital public services to make daily life easier. Large digital systems can widen access — and they also raise questions about privacy, inclusion, and who is left out.

cards.title: Lah
cards.body: In Singlish, lah is a common sentence-final particle. It colors a remark with attitude — emphasis, softness, or solidarity — depending on tone and context.

cards.title: A shared table
cards.body: A hawker meal is often eaten together at a simple table: satay, rice, broth, and other dishes that have been refined over years, at a price that keeps the room open.

places.name: Malta
places.note: Malta is more than a film backdrop or a beach party. It has a language of its own, quiet limestone streets in Mdina, and village festas that bring people into the square — and, since 2018, a vote at sixteen.

photos.caption_html: Fort St. Angelo in the Grand Harbour, with Valletta beyond. Photo: Mirror Project

photos.caption_html: A weathered doorway in Mdina. Photo: Mirror Project

cards.title: The festa
cards.body: The village festa is an annual parish celebration, typically a week of bands, processions, fireworks, and shared food. UNESCO inscribed the Maltese village festa in 2023.

cards.title: Voting at 16
cards.body: Since 2018, Maltese citizens who have turned sixteen can vote in general and European Parliament elections — one of the clearest ways young people here take part in public life.

cards.title: A language of its own
cards.body: Maltese is the only Semitic official language of the European Union, and the only one written in the Latin alphabet. Feeds often flatten the islands into a party backdrop; the language itself is a living reminder that Malta is not a set.

cards.title: Merħba
cards.body: Merħba is the Maltese word for welcome — a greeting that opens a door, a shop, or a conversation.

cards.title: Pastizzi
cards.body: Pastizzi are Malta’s beloved savoury pastries, typically filled with ricotta or peas, eaten standing at a shop window or shared on the way from one place to the next.

places.name: Hawaiʻi
places.note: Aloha is more than a greeting. In Hawaiʻi law it is described as mutual regard and affection, and young people have helped bring ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi back into daily life through Pūnana Leo immersion schools.

photos.alt: A sunset over a rocky shore, framed by trees
photos.caption_html: Sunset on a rocky shore, Hawaiʻi Island — the exact beach is unverified, so we hedge the place. Photo: Mirror Project

photos.alt: Palm trees silhouetted against a pink and purple sunset
photos.caption_html: Palms at sunset, Hawaiʻi. Photo: Mirror Project

cards.title: The Aloha Spirit
cards.body: Hawaiʻi law describes the Aloha Spirit as more than a greeting: mutual regard and affection, and a way of being careful with other people. State officials may give it consideration in their work.

cards.title: Pūnana Leo
cards.body: Pūnana Leo — “nest of voices” — are Hawaiian-language immersion preschools, begun in 1984, where children are raised in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi. Young people and families helped bring the language back into daily life.

cards.title: Not a backdrop
cards.body: Travel feeds often flatten Hawaiʻi into a resort sunset. Aloha, in Hawaiʻi law, is a practice of care, and the language revival is a reminder that this is a living culture, not a backdrop.

cards.title: ʻOhana
cards.body: ʻOhana means family, including the wider circle of relatives and people you care for — a word about belonging, not only about a household.

cards.title: Lūʻau and poke
cards.body: A lūʻau is a feast that brings people together. Poke — from a Hawaiian word for a cut piece — is seasoned raw fish, everyday food as well as something the wider world has borrowed.
